cases.question: If my ship sails from Rotterdam to Singapore, how much of that voyage's energy counts under FuelEU?
cases.answer: Half of it. For a voyage arriving at or departing from an EU port where the previous or next port of call is in a third country, FuelEU counts one half of the energy used; the whole voyage counts only between two EU ports. The regulation applies to ships above 5,000 GT carrying passengers or cargo commercially, whatever their flag.

cases.question: What GHG intensity does my ship need to stay under in 2030 under FuelEU?
cases.answer: From 1 January 2030 the yearly average GHG intensity of energy used on board must be at least 6% below the reference value of 91.16 gCO2eq/MJ, i.e. roughly 85.7 gCO2eq/MJ. The reduction started at 2% in 2025 and rises to 14.5% in 2035, 31% in 2040, 62% in 2045 and 80% in 2050.

cases.question: Is there a mandatory e-fuel quota under FuelEU, and when could it kick in?
cases.answer: Not a fixed one. A 2% RFNBO subtarget applies from 1 January 2034 only if the Commission's monitoring shows the RFNBO share of shipping energy was below 1% in 2031; it does not apply if evidence shows insufficient RFNBO capacity or availability, uneven distribution or too high a price. Until then RFNBO use is rewarded with a multiplier of 2 in the GHG intensity calculation from 2025 to the end of 2033.

cases.question: Our container ship is only alongside for about 90 minutes — do we still have to plug into shore power from 2030?
cases.answer: No. From 1 January 2030 containerships and passenger ships moored at the quayside in ports covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 must connect to onshore power for all their electrical demand at berth, but the requirement does not apply to ships moored for less than two hours, measured from the recorded times of arrival and departure.

cases.question: Can a ship that missed its GHG intensity target this year borrow compliance from next year, and what are the limits?
cases.answer: Yes. A company may borrow an advance compliance surplus from the following reporting period to cover a deficit; the borrowed amount multiplied by 1.1 is then subtracted from the ship's balance in that following period. It cannot borrow more than 2% of the GHG intensity limit multiplied by the ship's energy consumption, and cannot borrow in two consecutive reporting periods.

cases.question: How is the FuelEU penalty for a GHG intensity shortfall worked out, and does it get worse if we miss again the following year?
cases.answer: The penalty in EUR is |compliance balance| / (GHGIE_actual × 41 000) × 2 400: the compliance balance in gCO2eq, divided by the ship's actual GHG intensity to turn it back into MJ, then by 41 000 MJ per VLSFO-equivalent tonne, times EUR 2 400 per tonne, payable by 30 June of the verification period. If the ship has a deficit for two or more consecutive reporting periods, the amount is multiplied by 1 + (n − 1)/10, where n is the number of consecutive periods penalised.

cases.question: We operate a 3,000 GT general cargo ship calling at EU ports — is it caught by the EU MRV regulation?
cases.answer: Yes, since 1 January 2025. The MRV Regulation applies to ships of 5,000 GT and above, and from 2025 also to general cargo ships and offshore ships between 400 and 5,000 GT, for voyages to, from and within EU ports carrying cargo commercially. It covers CO2 and, for emissions from 2024 onwards, methane and nitrous oxide.

cases.question: A ship has just come under EU MRV for the first time — how long do we have to submit its monitoring plan, and who does it go to?
cases.answer: For a ship falling within scope for the first time after 1 January 2024, the company must submit a monitoring plan conforming to the Regulation to the administering authority responsible without undue delay and no later than three months after the ship's first call at a port under a Member State's jurisdiction; the administering authority approves it within four months of that first call. Under the original rules a plan for a new ship went to the verifier within two months of the first EU port call.

cases.question: Do we have to report every single voyage under MRV, or is there an exemption for ferries doing hundreds of trips a year?
cases.answer: Per-voyage monitoring (ports and times of departure and arrival, fuel consumed and emission factors, GHG emitted, distance, time at sea, cargo and transport work) is the default, but a ship is exempt from it if all its voyages in the reporting period start or end at a port under a Member State's jurisdiction and it performs more than 300 voyages in that period according to its schedule. Annual monitoring still applies.

cases.question: How long is an MRV document of compliance valid, and from when does a ship need to have one on board?
cases.answer: A document of compliance, issued by the verifier once the emissions report satisfies the Regulation, is valid for 18 months after the end of the reporting period. From 30 June of the year following the reporting period, a ship that made voyages in that period must carry a valid document of compliance on board when arriving at, within or departing from a port under a Member State's jurisdiction.

cases.question: What happens to a ship that keeps ignoring its MRV monitoring and reporting obligations year after year?
cases.answer: Member States must impose effective, proportionate and dissuasive penalties. If a ship has failed to comply for two or more consecutive reporting periods and other enforcement has failed, the competent authority of the port of entry may issue an expulsion order after hearing the company: every Member State except the flag State must then refuse the ship entry to its ports until the company complies, and a ship flying a Member State's flag is detained by that state. The shipowner has a right to a remedy before a court against the order.

cases.question: Once a verifier is accredited for EU MRV work, how long does the accreditation last and how is it kept in check?
cases.answer: The accreditation certificate issued by the national accreditation body is valid for at most five years. The accreditation body carries out annual surveillance of each accredited verifier, comprising at least an on-site visit and witnessing the work of a representative sample of the verifier's staff, with the first surveillance within 12 months of the certificate being issued; on the basis of that surveillance it decides whether accreditation continues.

cases.question: What materiality threshold does a FuelEU verifier apply, and can a misstatement below it still be treated as material?
cases.answer: The materiality level for verifying fuel and electricity consumption, distance travelled and time at sea and at berth in a FuelEU report is 5% of the respective total reported for each item in the reporting period. Misstatements or non-conformities below that level can still be treated as material where their scale, nature or the particular circumstances of their occurrence justify it, and the verifier must assess uncorrected ones individually and together for their impact.

cases.question: What format do we submit the MRV emissions report in — is there a mandatory template?
cases.answer: Yes. Companies must submit the emissions report and any partial emissions report using the electronic version of the template available in THETIS-MRV, which contains the information set out in Annex II of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2449.

cases.question: How should a ro-pax ferry work out 'cargo carried' for its MRV per-voyage monitoring?
cases.answer: For ro-pax ships, cargo carried is the number of passengers together with the mass of the cargo on board, where that mass may be the actual mass or the number of cargo units (trucks, cars, etc.) or occupied lane metres multiplied by default values for their weight.

cases.question: Our MRV verifier says it also has to identify inherent, control and detection risks as part of its risk analysis under Regulation (EU) 2015/757's implementing rules — what does Regulation (EU) 2015/757 itself require the verifier's risk analysis to check, on top of that?
cases.answer: Three things. It must identify potential risks related to the monitoring and reporting process by comparing the reported greenhouse gas emissions against estimated data derived from ship tracking data and characteristics such as installed engine power, carrying out further analysis where significant deviations are found. It must identify potential risks related to the different calculation steps by reviewing all the data sources and methodologies used. And it must take into account any effective risk control methods the company applies to reduce the uncertainty associated with the accuracy of its monitoring methods.

cases.question: If my ship sails from Rotterdam to Singapore, what share of that voyage's emissions do I need EU ETS allowances for?
cases.answer: Half. Surrender requirements apply to 50 % of the emissions from a voyage between a port of call under a Member State's jurisdiction and one outside it, in either direction. They apply to 100 % of emissions from voyages between two Member State ports and to 100 % of emissions within a Member State port of call.

cases.question: How many EU ETS allowances does a shipping company have to surrender for its 2025 emissions, and by what date?
cases.answer: Allowances covering 70 % of its verified 2025 emissions that fall under the surrender requirement, surrendered by 30 September 2026. The phase-in is 40 % of verified emissions reported for 2024, 70 % for 2025 and 100 % for 2026 and every year after, and Article 12(3) sets 30 September each year as the deadline for the preceding calendar year's emissions.

cases.question: Our charterer buys the fuel and decides the route and speed. Can we recover the EU ETS allowance cost from them, and who stays liable for surrendering?
cases.answer: Yes. Where another entity has taken on ultimate responsibility for buying the fuel, operating the ship, or both under a contractual arrangement, the shipping company is entitled to reimbursement from that entity for the costs of surrendering allowances. Operation of the ship means determining the cargo carried or the route and the speed. The shipping company nevertheless remains the entity responsible for surrendering allowances and for overall compliance.

cases.question: Which Member State administers a shipping company under the EU ETS if the company is registered outside the EU?
cases.answer: The Member State with the greatest estimated number of port calls from the company's voyages within the ETS scope over the preceding four monitoring years. If the company made no such voyage in those four years, it is the Member State where one of its ships started or ended its first voyage within the scope. A company registered in a Member State is administered by that Member State.

cases.question: Do ice-class ships get any relief on the EU ETS allowances they must surrender?
cases.answer: Yes. Shipping companies may surrender 5 % fewer allowances than the verified emissions released until 31 December 2030 from ice-class ships, provided the ships have ice class IA or IA Super, or an equivalent ice class established on the basis of HELCOM Recommendation 25/7.

cases.question: Are ferry voyages to small islands exempt from EU ETS surrender obligations, and where are the islands listed?
cases.answer: They can be. At a Member State's request the Commission provides, by implementing act, that no action is taken against shipping companies for emissions released until 31 December 2030 from voyages by passenger ships other than cruise ships, and by ro-pax ships, between a port of an island with no road or rail link to the mainland and fewer than 200 000 permanent residents and a port of the same Member State, and from those ships' activities in port for such voyages. The islands and ports are listed in Annex I to Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2895.

cases.question: What happens if a shipping company does not surrender enough EU ETS allowances?
cases.answer: It pays an excess emissions penalty of EUR 100 for each tonne of CO2 equivalent not covered, and paying does not release it from surrendering allowances for those excess emissions the following year. If it fails to meet its surrender obligations for two or more consecutive reporting periods and other enforcement has failed, the competent authority of the Member State of the port of entry may, after hearing the company, issue an expulsion order. Every Member State except the flag State then refuses the company's ships entry to its ports until the obligations are met, and a ship flying a Member State's flag is detained by that State.

cases.question: MRV borrows its definition of 'company' from Article 3, point (w) of Directive 2003/87/EC — what does that provision say?
cases.answer: Article 3, point (w) of Directive 2003/87/EC defines 'shipping company' as the shipowner or any other organisation or person, such as the manager or the bareboat charterer, that has assumed the responsibility for the operation of the ship from the shipowner and that, on assuming such responsibility, has agreed to take over all the duties and responsibilities imposed by the ISM Code, set out in Annex I to Regulation (EC) No 336/2006.

cases.question: For the EU ETS, does a container ship's stop at Tanger Med count as a port of call?
cases.answer: No. The Directive's definition of port of call excludes stops of containerships in a neighbouring container transhipment port listed in the implementing act adopted under Article 3ga(2). Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2297 lists two such ports: East Port Said in Egypt and Tanger Med in Morocco.

cases.question: Does the EU ETS have its own monitoring and verification rules for ship emissions, or does it rely on the MRV Regulation?
cases.answer: It relies on MRV. The administering authority ensures that a shipping company monitors and reports the relevant parameters and submits aggregated emissions data at company level in accordance with Chapter II of Regulation (EU) 2015/757, and that this data is verified under the verification and accreditation rules in Chapter III of that Regulation. Under Article 11a of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 the verified aggregated data at company level goes to the administering authority by 31 March each year.

cases.question: How does the penalty for an EU ETS allowance shortfall compare with the FuelEU penalty for a compliance deficit?
cases.answer: The ETS penalty is EUR 100 for each tonne of CO2 equivalent for which allowances were not surrendered, and the company must still surrender the missing allowances the following year. The FuelEU penalty is |compliance balance| / (GHGIE_actual × 41 000) × 2 400 EUR: the deficit in gCO2eq divided by the ship's actual GHG intensity to give MJ, converted to VLSFO-equivalent tonnes at 41 000 MJ per tonne and multiplied by EUR 2 400 per tonne, and it is multiplied by 1 + (n − 1)/10 when the ship has a deficit for two or more consecutive reporting periods.

cases.question: What CII rating band does a ship fall into if its attained CII is 5% above the required value?
What price-difference figure between RFNBO and fossil fuel is currently used in the FuelEU RFNBO penalty formula?
Has Maersk been fined under FuelEU yet, and how much did it pay?
What is the maximum weight of hand luggage allowed on Ryanair flights?
FuelEU keeps talking about voyages but never seems to say what one is — what actually counts as a voyage?
cases.answer: FuelEU does not define it itself. Article 3, point (11) takes 'voyage' from Article 3, point (c) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757, where a voyage is any movement of a ship that originates from or terminates in a port of call. So a movement counts as a voyage as long as a port of call sits at one end of it or the other.

cases.question: Our ship is right on the 5,000 GT line — which tonnage figure decides whether FuelEU catches us?
cases.answer: FuelEU applies to ships above 5 000 gross tonnage that transport passengers or cargo for commercial purposes, whatever their flag (Article 2(1)). 'Gross tonnage' is not defined in FuelEU: Article 3, point (14) takes it from Article 3, point (e) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757, which is the tonnage calculated in accordance with the tonnage measurement regulations in Annex I to the IMO International Convention on Tonnage Measurement of Ships of 1969, or any successor convention. So it is the ITC 1969 gross tonnage on the ship's tonnage certificate that matters, not a deadweight or net figure.

cases.question: We're anchored inside the port limits, hotelling while we wait for a berth to free up — is the ship 'at berth' as far as FuelEU is concerned?
cases.answer: Yes. Article 3, point (15) of FuelEU takes 'ship at berth' from Article 3, point (n) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757: a ship which is securely moored or anchored in a port falling under the jurisdiction of a Member State while it is loading, unloading or hotelling, including the time spent when not engaged in cargo operations. Anchored counts, and hotelling is named expressly, so the ship is at berth. FuelEU then gives that situation its own name in Article 3, point (16): a 'ship at anchorage' is a ship at berth which is not moored at the quayside.

cases.question: If our containership rides at anchorage instead of coming alongside, does the 2030 shore-power obligation still bite?
cases.answer: No. Article 6(1) applies to a ship moored at the quayside in a port of call covered by Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2023/1804 under the jurisdiction of a Member State. A ship at anchorage is defined in Article 3, point (16) as a ship at berth which is not moored at the quayside, and 'ship at berth' itself comes from Article 3, point (n) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757. Because the ship is not moored at the quayside, the OPS obligation in Article 6 is not triggered — although the energy used during the stay still falls within scope under Article 2(1), point (a).

cases.question: Our containership stops at Tanger Med to tranship boxes before running up to Algeciras — does the Tanger Med stop count as a port of call under FuelEU?
cases.answer: No. Article 3, point (10) excludes from 'port of call' stops of containerships in a neighbouring container transhipment port listed in the implementing act adopted pursuant to Article 2(2). Article 2(2) required the Commission to establish that list, which is set out in the Annex to Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/1127 and names two ports: East Port Said in Egypt and Tanger Med in Morocco. So for a containership the Tanger Med stop is not a port of call.

cases.question: Our verifier says the ship finished the year with a compliance surplus — what is that exactly, and where does the number come from?
cases.answer: Article 3, point (36) defines a compliance surplus as a compliance balance with a positive value; point (37) makes a negative one a compliance deficit. 'Compliance balance' is itself defined in point (35) as the measure of a ship's over- or under-compliance with the limits for the yearly average GHG intensity of the energy used on board or the RFNBO subtarget, calculated in accordance with Part A of Annex IV. So the number is the Part A calculation, and a positive result is the surplus.

cases.question: We run fuel cells at berth rather than plugging in — does that get us out of the FuelEU shore-power requirement?
cases.answer: It can. Article 6(5), point (b) disapplies the OPS obligation for ships that use zero-emission technologies for all their electrical power demand at berth while moored at the quayside, provided those technologies comply with the general requirements in Annex III and are listed and specified in the delegated and implementing acts adopted under Article 6(6) and (7). 'Zero-emission technology' is defined in Article 3, point (7) as a technology that, when used to provide energy, does not release CO2, CH4, N2O, SOx, NOx or particulate matter into the atmosphere by ships. Annex III lists power supplied by onboard fuel cells, with a fuel or a system ensuring that no such emissions are released when the energy is provided.

cases.question: How do we work out the shore-power penalty for our ship — where does the power figure in it actually come from?
cases.answer: Article 23(5) sets the penalty at EUR 1,5 multiplied by the established total electrical power demand of the ship at berth and by the total number of hours, rounded up to the nearest whole hour, spent at berth in non-compliance with Article 6. That power term is defined in Article 3, point (26) as the highest value, in kilowatts, of the ship's total demand for electricity at berth, including hotel and cargo handling workloads. The figure itself is the one recorded in the monitoring plan under Article 8(3), point (e): the value in the ship's electrical load balance or load study used to demonstrate compliance with Regulations 40 and 41 of SOLAS Chapter II-1, or, if the ship cannot provide that reference, 25 % of the total of the maximum continuous ratings of the main engines.

cases.question: Can we put a ship into a FuelEU compliance pool if its document of compliance is not sorted?
cases.answer: No. Article 21(5) says a ship shall not be included in a pool if it does not comply with the obligation set out in Article 24 — holding a valid FuelEU document of compliance by 30 June of the verification period, which applies to ships calling at, arriving at, staying within or departing from a port under a Member State's jurisdiction, or which carried out voyages during the corresponding reporting period. Separately, Article 21(4) makes a pool valid only if the total pooled compliance is positive, no ship that had a deficit ends up with a bigger one after allocation, and no ship that had a surplus ends up in deficit.

cases.question: Our IA-class ship spent part of the winter pushing through ice — can we take that extra fuel out of the FuelEU calculation?
cases.answer: Yes, through Annex V, which calculates the adjusted mass of fuel for ice navigation: the additional energy consumption due to the technical characteristics of a ship of ice class IA or IA Super or equivalent, the additional energy consumption due to sailing in ice conditions for a ship of ice class IC, IB, IA or IA Super or equivalent, and the resulting adjusted mass allocated to each fuel. The terms it turns on sit in Article 3: 'ice class' is the notation assigned by the flag State or a recognised organisation (point (21)), 'ice edge' is the demarcation between open sea and sea ice as set out in paragraph 4.4.8 of the WMO Sea-Ice Nomenclature of March 2014 (point (22)), and 'sailing in ice conditions' is sailing by an ice-class ship in a sea area within the ice edge (point (23)).

cases.question: MRV says to monitor emissions per voyage and annually by applying the appropriate method — which methods does it mean, and where are they set out?
cases.answer: Article 8 requires companies, on the basis of the monitoring plan assessed under Article 13(1), to monitor greenhouse gas emissions for each ship on a per-voyage and an annual basis by applying an appropriate method from among those set out in Part B of Annex I, and by calculating the emissions in accordance with Part A of Annex I. So Article 8 itself carries neither list: Part B of Annex I holds the monitoring methods and Part A holds the calculation rules.

cases.question: Our ship comes under FuelEU for the first time next month — when is the monitoring plan due, and does it have to be on a set form?
cases.answer: For a ship falling within scope for the first time after 31 August 2024, Article 8(2) of FuelEU requires the company to submit a monitoring plan to the verifier without undue delay and no later than two months after the ship's first call at a port under the jurisdiction of a Member State. The form is not optional: Article 1(1) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2024/2031 requires companies to use an electronic version of the template set out in its Annex, accessible in the FuelEU database, and Article 1(2) requires verifiers to use the same template when recording the assessed plan in the database under Article 11(3) of FuelEU.

cases.question: What happens if we miss the deadline for submitting our aggregated emissions data at company level?
cases.answer: Article 11a(2) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 requires companies, from 2025, to submit verified aggregated emissions data at company level to the administering authority responsible by 31 March each year, covering the previous year's reporting period; under Article 11a(3) that authority may require it earlier, but not before 28 February. If nothing arrives by the deadline, Article 2(1), point (a) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2849 requires the administering authority responsible to make a conservative estimate of the aggregated emissions data at company level. It must do the same where the data submitted is found not to comply with Regulation (EU) 2015/757, or has not been verified as satisfactory. The authority then informs the company whether and which corrections are required, and the company must make that information available to the verifier.

cases.question: Where do we actually register a FuelEU compliance pool, and what is the database meant to do for us?
cases.answer: Registration happens in the FuelEU database. Under Article 21(2) of FuelEU the company registers its intention to include a ship's compliance balance in a pool, the allocation of the total pool compliance balance to each ship, and the verifier chosen to verify that allocation; where the ships are controlled by two or more companies, Article 21(3) requires all of them to validate those details in the database, and Article 21(8) requires the selected verifier to record the definitive composition and allocation by 30 April of the verification period. Article 5(5) of Regulation (EU) 2026/394 is what obliges the database to carry that functionality: a pooling function letting companies and verifiers pool the compliance balances of different ships and register and verify the pool's composition and the allocation to each ship.

cases.question: What does a national accreditation body actually examine when it accredits a FuelEU verifier?
cases.answer: Under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2025/192, during the accreditation process and annual surveillance the national accreditation body assesses whether the verifier and its personnel have the competence to assess monitoring plans, verify FuelEU reports and partial FuelEU reports, verify conformity with the GHG intensity requirements by calculating the GHG intensity of the energy used on board, the compliance balance and non-compliant port calls, and issue a FuelEU document of compliance; whether they apply complete and effective verification methods for that work; and whether they meet the requirements for verifiers in Chapter IV of the implementing regulation on FuelEU verification activities, including impartiality and independence. Article 4(2) requires the applicant to make available, before the assessment begins, the procedures and processes and the quality management system referred to in Article 35 of that implementing regulation. Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/2027 in turn requires documented procedures for the verification activities in Articles 4 to 29 and a quality management system covering policies and responsibilities, management review, internal audits, corrective actions, actions to address risks and opportunities and preventive actions, and control of documented information.

cases.question: We operate a ro-pax ferry between the Greek mainland and an island of about 20,000 people. Can that route be exempted from FuelEU, and for how long?
cases.answer: Yes, but only if the Member State grants it. A Member State may exempt specific routes and ports for passenger ships other than cruise ships sailing between its own ports and an island port under its jurisdiction with fewer than 200,000 permanent residents. The exemption covers the energy used on those voyages and during the stay in the island's port. The Member State must notify the exemption to the Commission before it takes effect, and the Commission publishes it in the Official Journal. No such exemption applies beyond 31 December 2029.

cases.question: We're looking at fitting onboard carbon capture on one of our tankers. Would the captured CO2 bring down our FuelEU GHG intensity?
cases.answer: Not under the current rules. The GHG intensity formula in Annex I counts well-to-tank and tank-to-wake emissions of the fuel used, with a reward factor only for wind-assisted propulsion. It has no term for captured carbon. Article 30(2)(i) only requires the Commission, in its review due by 31 December 2027 and every five years after, to consider including new abatement technologies such as onboard carbon capture in the GHG intensity and compliance balance calculations, subject to a verifiable method for monitoring and accounting for the captured carbon.

cases.question: If the 2% RFNBO subtarget kicks in from 2034, can we meet it with advanced biofuels like UCO biodiesel instead of e-fuels?
cases.answer: Not with UCO biodiesel. Article 5(9) lets a ship escape the subtarget if it shows the same share of its yearly energy is met by other fuels that give equivalent GHG emissions savings and are certified under Article 10. Biofuels from the feedstocks in Part B of Annex IX to the Renewable Energy Directive are excluded, and that Part lists used cooking oil. Other certified fuels with equivalent savings can count.

cases.question: Once our cruise ship is plugged into shore power, do we also have to shut down the oil-fired boilers while we're alongside?
cases.answer: No. The shore-power obligation in Article 6 requires the ship to connect to OPS and use it for all its electrical power demand at berth, which Article 3(25) defines as the demand for electricity to meet all energy needs based on electricity on board. Oil-fired boilers meet a non-electrical need, so they are not caught. The fuel they burn at berth still counts as energy used in the port of call, and boilers are among the fuel consumer units in the Annex I GHG intensity calculation.

cases.question: We run a con-ro that carries both containers and trailers. Does the 2030 FuelEU shore-power requirement apply to us?
cases.answer: No, unless it is a passenger ship. The shore-power obligations in Article 6(1) to (3) apply only to containerships and passenger ships. Article 3(31) defines a containership as a ship designed exclusively for the carriage of containers in holds and on deck, so a con-ro that also carries trailers falls outside.

cases.question: The terminal had no shore power available at our berth this call. Are we exempt, and is there a limit on how often we can use that excuse?
cases.answer: Yes, for that call. Article 6(5)(d) exempts ships unable to connect because the port has no OPS connection point available, and the competent authority records the exception in the FuelEU database. From 1 January 2035, in ports covered by Article 9 of the AFIR Regulation, this exception and the grid-stability and incompatibility ones ((e) and (f)) can together cover at most 10% of the ship's port calls in the reporting period, rounded up, or 10 port calls, whichever is lower. A call does not count towards that cap if the company shows, from the advance information exchanged with the port, that it could not reasonably have known the ship would be unable to connect.

cases.question: Which FuelEU default emission factors do we use for the VLSFO we bunker?
cases.answer: FuelEU has no VLSFO category. Annex II sets fossil fuel defaults by ISO 8217 grade, so it depends on the grade on the bunker delivery note. RME to RMK (HFO): LCV 0.0405 MJ/g, WtT 13.5 gCO2eq/MJ, Cf CO2 3.114 g/g. RMA to RMD (LFO): LCV 0.041, WtT 13.2, Cf CO2 3.151. DMX to DMB (MDO/MGO): LCV 0.0427, WtT 14.4, Cf CO2 3.206. All three use Cf CH4 0.00005 and Cf N2O 0.00018 for all ICEs. For fossil fuels the well-to-tank defaults cannot be replaced with actual values.

cases.question: Our engine maker says our dual-fuel engine slips far less methane than the FuelEU default. Can we use a lower slip figure, and what is the default we'd otherwise get?
cases.answer: Yes, if it is certified. Article 10(5) lets a company diverge from the Annex II tank-to-wake defaults, except the tank-to-wake CO2 factors of fossil fuels, where actual values are certified by laboratory testing or direct emissions measurement. The method goes in the monitoring plan and is assessed by the verifier. The Annex II LNG slip defaults (Cslip, as % of fuel mass, at 50% engine load) are 3.1% for Otto dual-fuel medium speed, 1.7% for Otto dual-fuel slow speed, 0.2% for Diesel dual-fuel slow speed and 2.6% for LBSI engines.

cases.question: Under FuelEU do we have to record fuel for every voyage, or can we just report yearly totals? And when is the report due to our verifier?
cases.answer: Every voyage and port call. From 1 January 2025, Article 15(1) requires companies to monitor and record, for each ship arriving at or departing from a port of call and for each voyage in scope, the ports and times, fuel consumed at berth and at sea by type, OPS electricity, the emission factors and substitute energy used. They compile this annually, and by 31 January of the verification period they give the verifier a ship-specific FuelEU report containing it.

cases.question: If one of our ships is in a FuelEU pool, can it also borrow compliance from next year, and can it be in two pools at once?
cases.answer: No to borrowing, and only one pool per target. Article 21(7) says Article 20(2), the borrowing of an advance compliance surplus, does not apply to a ship in a pool. A ship's compliance balance cannot be in more than one pool in the same reporting period, though two separate pools may be used, one for the GHG intensity target and one for the RFNBO subtarget. Any surplus the ship ends up with after pooling can still be banked under Article 20(1).

cases.question: Our time charterer buys all the fuel and sets the route. Can we pass the FuelEU penalty on to them, and who is actually liable to pay it?
cases.answer: The company stays liable. It must pay the FuelEU penalty to its administering State by 30 June of the verification period. Article 23(8) lets it agree contractually that the commercial operator reimburses it, where the operator is responsible for buying the fuel or operating the ship, meaning deciding the cargo, route and speed. Article 23(9) allows the same with fuel suppliers. Neither agreement moves the legal responsibility off the company.

cases.question: We're fitting rotor sails that give about 10% of our propulsion power. How much does that cut our FuelEU GHG intensity?
cases.answer: About 3%. Annex I multiplies the GHG intensity result by a wind reward factor based on P_wind/P_prop: 0.99 at 0.05, 0.97 at 0.1 and 0.95 at 0.15 or more. A ratio of 0.1 gives 0.97. P_wind is the available effective power of the wind-assisted propulsion systems, calculated under the IMO EEDI/EEXI guidance on innovative technologies (MEPC.1/Circ.896), and P_prop is the ship's propulsion power.

cases.question: What has to go into the verification report our MRV verifier issues, and what makes it come out satisfactory?
cases.answer: Article 13 of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 sets the outcome: where the verifier concludes with reasonable assurance that the emissions report is free from material misstatements it issues a verification report stating the report has been verified as satisfactory, specifying all issues relevant to the work carried out; where misstatements or non-conformities were communicated and not corrected and, individually or combined, lead to material misstatements, the verifier issues a report stating that the emissions report does not comply. Article 22 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 holds the contents: the report goes to the company, which submits it with the emissions report to the administering authority responsible, and it must include a statement verifying the report as satisfactory or unsatisfactory, along with the company name and IMO unique company and registered owner identification number and identification of the ship, a title making clear it is a verification report, the identity of the verifier and a contact person, the objectives and scope of the verification, a reference to the emissions report and reporting period, a reference to the monitoring plans assessed as satisfactory, the verification standards used, a summary of the verifier's procedures including site visits, and a verification statement.

cases.question: Under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, what does a ship pay per tonne of CO2 equivalent if it misses the direct compliance target?
How many ships did the Paris MoU detain for MRV-related deficiencies last year?
What reduction factor applies when calculating the required EEXI for a 60,000 DWT bulk carrier?
Under the IMO Data Collection System, by what date must a company submit a ship's annual fuel oil consumption data to its flag State?
From what date does the UK ETS cover domestic maritime voyages, and which ships does it apply to?
Does FuelEU apply when my ship calls at Norwegian or Icelandic ports, or only at EU ones?
What fleet data and method was the 91.16 g/MJ FuelEU reference value calculated from?
What's the going rate per tonne CO2e to buy surplus into a FuelEU pool for a ship in deficit?
We burn B30 on a Rotterdam to Houston run. Can we allocate all of the bio part to the half of the energy that counts under FuelEU?

When looking at the Thetis MRV download for 2025, in order to arrive at the gross number of CO2 tonnes to be surrendered against, I should add the total reportable CO2 columns of both the Full ERs and the Partial ER tabs of the MRV dataset (and apply the 70% phase-in for last year). True or False? I get 61.8 full ER plus 2.48 million Partial ERs from the latest download.
cases.answer: True on the law, with one caveat the regulations cannot settle. The figure to surrender against is each ship's total aggregated emissions to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, calculated under Annex II Part C of Regulation (EU) 2015/757: the amount within the Article 3ga scope (100 % of emissions on voyages between EU ports and within them, 50 % of voyages to or from a port outside the EU), less the Article 12(3) derogations, with the Article 3gb phase-in applied, which is 40 % of verified emissions reported for 2024, 70 % for 2025 and 100 % from 2026. A partial report is the verified report the previous company submits on a change of company for the part of the year the ship was under its responsibility (Article 11(2)), and company totals are built from the emissions reports and those partial reports together (Article 11a(1)), so a fleet total takes both. The dataset settles the rest: in the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15) the column to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC carries no phase-in, since each ship's figure equals 100 % of voyages between EU ports and at berth plus 50 % of voyages to or from them. Full reports total 88.26 Mt and partial reports 3.55 Mt, 91.80 Mt together, and 70 % of that is 64.26 Mt. The 61.8 and 2.48 million quoted are already 70 % of the columns, so applying the phase-in again would count it twice.

cases.question: Per the THETIS-MRV data, how many tonnes of CO2 did shipping companies have to surrender allowances for, for 2024?
cases.answer: About 36.3 Mt. The 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19) totals 87.56 Mt on full reports and 3.20 Mt on partial reports, 90.76 Mt together, and under Article 3gb only 40 % of 2024 emissions are surrendered for.

cases.question: What was the total CO2 reported by ships in THETIS-MRV for 2025?
cases.answer: 150.99 Mt on full emissions reports and 5.91 Mt on partial reports, 156.90 Mt together, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: How many emissions reports were filed in THETIS-MRV for 2024?
cases.answer: 15,195: 14,168 full emissions reports and 1,027 partial emissions reports, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19).

cases.question: How much CO2 is to be reported under the EU ETS for 2025, according to THETIS-MRV?
cases.answer: 91.80 Mt to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC: 88.26 Mt on full emissions reports and 3.55 Mt on partial reports, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: How much CO2 did ships emit at berth in EU ports in 2024, per the MRV data?
cases.answer: 7.59 Mt within Member State ports at berth: 7.31 Mt on full emissions reports and 0.28 Mt on partial reports, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19).

cases.question: What were CO2 emissions from voyages between EU ports in 2025 in the MRV dataset?
cases.answer: 39.77 Mt on voyages between Member State ports: 38.52 Mt on full emissions reports and 1.25 Mt on partial reports, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: What share of ships' total reported CO2 in 2025 falls under the EU ETS?
cases.answer: About 58.5 %: 91.80 Mt to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC out of 156.90 Mt total CO2, full and partial emissions reports together, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: Did total CO2 reported by ships in THETIS-MRV go up or down between 2024 and 2025, and by how much?
cases.answer: Up, by about 4.26 Mt (2.8 %): from 152.64 Mt in the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19) to 156.90 Mt in the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15), full and partial emissions reports together.

cases.question: What proportion of the 2025 MRV emissions reports were partial reports?
cases.answer: About 8.1 %: 1,520 partial emissions reports out of 18,697 in all (17,177 full), per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: In 2024, were MRV emissions on voyages arriving at EU ports higher than on voyages departing from them?
cases.answer: Yes: 56.09 Mt on voyages arriving at Member State ports against 51.66 Mt on voyages departing from them, full and partial emissions reports together, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19).

cases.question: Based on THETIS-MRV, how many tonnes of CO2 will shipping companies have to surrender allowances for, for 2025?
cases.answer: About 64.26 Mt. The 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15) totals 88.26 Mt on full reports and 3.55 Mt on partial reports to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, 91.80 Mt together, and under Article 3gb 70 % of 2025 emissions are surrendered for.

cases.question: If shipping's ETS-reportable emissions in 2026 were the same as in 2025 per THETIS-MRV, how many tonnes would be surrendered for 2026?
cases.answer: The whole 91.80 Mt: from 2026 Article 3gb makes shipping companies liable to surrender allowances for 100 % of verified emissions, and the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15) has 91.80 Mt to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC.

cases.question: Is the 70% phase-in already applied to the 'to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC' figure in the 2025 MRV data?
cases.answer: No. The figure is the full amount within the ETS scope: across the 2025 reports it sits at a median of 1.00 times 100 % of emissions between Member State ports and at berth plus 50 % of voyages departing from or arriving at them. The Article 3gb phase-in, 70 % for 2025, applies at surrender, and the Union Registry likewise takes company-level emissions for 2024 and 2025 before the application of Article 3gb, calculating those percentages automatically.

cases.question: Does the EU ETS column in the THETIS-MRV data already count only half of emissions on voyages to or from non-EU ports?
cases.answer: Yes. Article 3ga applies the ETS to 50 % of emissions on voyages departing from or arriving at a Member State port from outside the EU, and 100 % between Member State ports and at berth; the dataset's ETS figure sits at a median of 1.00 times that split in both the 2024 and 2025 files, with 76 % and 80 % of reports within 1 % of it, the rest mostly derogations.

cases.question: What was the Carras Hellas' exposure to EU ETS in 2024?
cases.answer: About 7,813 t. Carras (Hellas) S.A. (IMO company number 0606585) reported 19,533 t of CO2 to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC on 7 full emissions reports for 2024, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19), and under Article 3gb shipping companies surrender for 40 % of 2024 emissions.

cases.question: Which Carras Hellas ships reported under MRV in 2024?
cases.answer: Seven bulk carriers under Carras (Hellas) S.A., per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19): DONNA ALEXANDRA (IMO 9950595), AQUALIBRA (9765603), JOHN M CARRAS (9592707), ADRIANA ROSE (9727467), ARIETTA LILY (9727479), ATHINA CARRAS (9592719) and AQUAGEMINI (9757010).

cases.question: What will Maersk A/S have to surrender for 2025?
cases.answer: Allowances for about 2.40 Mt of CO2. Maersk A/S (IMO company number 5808451) reported 3,435,479 t to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC for 2025 on 166 reports, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15), and under Article 3gb 70 % of 2025 emissions are surrendered for.

cases.question: What is Hapag-Lloyd's EU ETS exposure for 2025?
cases.answer: About 689,971 t of CO2. Hapag-Lloyd AG (IMO company number 0217944) reported 985,672 t to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC for 2025 on 64 reports, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15), and under Article 3gb 70 % of 2025 emissions are surrendered for.

cases.question: List the top 5 ships by EU ETS emissions in 2024
cases.answer: By CO2 to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19): CRUISE BARCELONA (IMO 9351488, Grimaldi Euromed) 124,615 t, CRUISE ROMA (9351476, Grimaldi Euromed) 109,712 t, MSC WORLD EUROPA (9837420, MSC Cruise Management UK) 106,376 t, SUPERFAST XI (9227417, Superfast Ferries) 105,445 t and MSC FANTASIA (9359791, MSC Cruise Management UK) 105,432 t.

cases.question: How much did Emma Maersk emit in 2025?
cases.answer: EMMA MAERSK (IMO 9321483, Maersk A/S) reported 95,176 t of total CO2 for 2025, 49,908 t of it to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: What CO2 emissions did the ship with IMO number 9321483 report in THETIS-MRV for 2024?
cases.answer: EMMA MAERSK (IMO 9321483, Maersk A/S) reported 90,420 t of total CO2 for 2024, 51,024 t of it to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, on one full emissions report, per the 2024 file (version 243 of 2026-09-19).

cases.question: What were total CO2 emissions reported by ships in THETIS-MRV for 2023?
Which shipping company reported the most CO2 in THETIS-MRV for 2025?
cases.answer: MSC Shipmanagement Ltd (IMO company number 1535947): 9.03 Mt of total CO2 on 440 reports, 5.38 Mt of it to be reported under Directive 2003/87/EC, the most on either measure; Maersk A/S is next with 6.40 Mt and 3.44 Mt, per the 2025 file (version 58 of 2026-09-15).

cases.question: How is the GHG intensity of the energy used on board calculated under FuelEU?
cases.answer: By Equation (1) in Annex I: GHG intensity [gCO2eq/MJ] = f_wind × (WtT + TtW). WtT is the sum over fuels i of M_i × CO2eq,WtT,i × LCV_i, plus the sum over OPS connection points k of E_k × CO2eq,electricity,k, divided by the sum over fuels of M_i × LCV_i × RWD_i plus the sum of E_k. The electricity term in that numerator is set to zero, so shore power adds energy to the denominator but no emissions. TtW is the sum over fuels i and fuel consumer units j of M_i,j × [(1 − C_slip,j/100) × CO2eq,TtW,i,j + (C_slip,j/100) × CO2eq,TtW,slip,i,j], over the same denominator. M is fuel mass in grams, LCV the lower calorific value in MJ/g, E_k the electricity delivered at berth in MJ, C_slip the percentage of fuel that slips uncombusted, RWD_i the RFNBO reward factor of 2 from 2025 to the end of 2033 (otherwise 1), and f_wind the reward factor for wind-assisted propulsion.

cases.question: How do I turn my ship's FuelEU compliance balance into a penalty amount in euros?
cases.answer: The compliance balance in gCO2eq is (GHGIE_target − GHGIE_actual) × (the sum over fuels i of M_i × LCV_i plus the sum of electricity E_k delivered at berth), so the gap to the limit times the energy used. The penalty in EUR is |compliance balance| / (GHGIE_actual × 41 000) × 2 400. Dividing by the actual GHG intensity turns the deficit back into MJ of energy, dividing by 41 000 converts that into metric tonnes of VLSFO equivalent (one tonne of VLSFO being 41 000 MJ), and each such tonne costs EUR 2 400.

cases.question: Under the EU MRV Regulation, how do I calculate my ship's CO2 emissions from its fuel consumption, and does slipped methane count towards the CO2 figure?
cases.answer: CO2 is the sum over fuels i of (M_i − M_i,NC) × EF_CO2,i, where M_i is the total mass of fuel i used across all emission sources, M_i,NC the mass of that fuel not combusted but released to the atmosphere, and EF_CO2,i its tank-to-wake CO2 emission factor from the table in point 2. M_i,NC is the fuel mass used in each emission source j times that source's slippage coefficient, M_i,j × C_j / 100, summed. So slipped fuel is taken out of the CO2 figure and counted as methane instead: CH4 is the sum of (M_i − M_i,NC) × EF_CH4,i plus the slip CH4_S = M_i,NC. Total reported GHG in tonnes CO2 equivalent is CO2 + CH4 × GWP_CH4 + N2O × GWP_N2O.

cases.question: Under RED, how are the emissions of a bioliquid-fired cogeneration plant allocated to the useful heat it delivers alongside electricity?
cases.answer: EC_h = (E / η_h) × (C_h × η_h) / (C_el × η_el + C_h × η_h). E is the total GHG emissions of the bioliquid before end-conversion, η_h and η_el are the annual heat and electrical efficiencies (useful heat or electricity out divided by fuel energy in), C_el is the exergy fraction of electricity, set to 1, and C_h is the Carnot efficiency of the heat, (T_h − T_0) / T_h, with T_h the delivery temperature of the heat in kelvin and T_0 = 273.15 K. Heat exported for heating buildings below 150 °C may instead use C_h = 0.3546. The electricity takes the matching share, EC_el = (E / η_el) × (C_el × η_el) / (C_el × η_el + C_h × η_h), and a heat-only installation uses EC_h = E / η_h.

cases.question: Under CBAM, how are the specific embedded emissions of a complex good calculated when it is made from imported precursors?
cases.answer: SEE_g = (AttrEm_g + EE_InpMat) / AL_g, in tonnes CO2e per tonne of the good. AttrEm_g is the installation's attributed emissions for the good, DirEm + IndirEm, meaning direct emissions plus indirect emissions from the electricity consumed, within the system boundaries of the production process. AL_g is the activity level, the quantity of the good produced in the reporting period. EE_InpMat is the sum over precursors i of M_i × SEE_i, the mass of each precursor used times its specific embedded emissions. Only precursors listed in Annex I and originating in third countries not exempted under Annex III count. For a simple good the precursor term drops out and SEE_g = AttrEm_g / AL_g.

cases.question: If the FuelEU RFNBO subtarget applies and my ship falls short of it, how are the shortfall and the penalty calculated?
cases.answer: The shortfall is the ship's RFNBO compliance balance in MJ: CB_RFNBO = 0.02 × (the sum over all fuels i of M_i × LCV_i) − (the sum over RFNBO fuels i of M_i × LCV_i), so 2 % of the yearly energy used on board minus the energy drawn from RFNBO or from fuels certified as giving equivalent GHG savings. If CB_RFNBO > 0, the penalty in EUR is CB_RFNBO / 41 000 × P_d, where 41 000 MJ is one metric tonne of VLSFO equivalent and P_d is the price difference between RFNBO and fossil fuel compatible with the ship's installation, calculated by a method the Commission sets in implementing acts. The 2 % subtarget only applies from 1 January 2034, and only if RFNBO made up less than 1 % of the energy used on board by ships in the 2031 reporting period.

cases.question: Under the EU MRV Regulation, how do I combine my ship's CO2, methane and nitrous oxide into one greenhouse gas figure in CO2 equivalent?
cases.answer: GHG_MRV = CO2_MRV + CH4_MRV × GWP_CH4 + N2O_MRV × GWP_N2O, in tonnes of CO2 equivalent. CO2_MRV is the sum over fuels i of (M_i − M_i,NC) × EF_CO2,i. CH4_MRV is the sum over fuels i of (M_i − M_i,NC) × EF_CH4,i plus CH4_S, the methane released uncombusted, which is set equal to M_i,NC. N2O_MRV is the sum over fuels i of (M_i − M_i,NC) × EF_N2O,i. M_i is the total mass of fuel i used, and M_i,NC the mass not combusted, the sum over fuels i and emission sources j of M_i,j × C_j / 100 with C_j the slippage coefficient in percent. The emission factors are the tank-to-wake factors in the table under point 2 of that Part of Annex I. GWP_CH4 and GWP_N2O are the 100-year global warming potentials in the Annex to Delegated Regulation (EU) 2020/1044: 28 for CH4 and 265 for N2O, not values taken from another act.

cases.question: We operate a 6,500 GT offshore supply vessel working out of Esbjerg. Do we have to surrender ETS allowances for it already, or only from a later year?
cases.answer: Only from 2027. Annex I of the ETS Directive brings in the maritime transport activities covered by Regulation (EU) 2015/757, except, until 31 December 2026, those covered by Article 2(1b) of that Regulation. Article 2(1b) is the provision that brought offshore ships of 5 000 gross tonnage and above into MRV from 1 January 2025. So the vessel is monitored and reported under MRV now, but its emissions fall under the ETS only from 1 January 2027.

cases.question: Our LNG carriers have some methane slip. Do we need ETS allowances for the methane as well as the CO2, and from which year?
cases.answer: Yes, from 2026. Annex I of the ETS Directive lists carbon dioxide as the greenhouse gas for maritime transport and adds methane and nitrous oxide from 1 January 2026, so methane emitted from 2026 onwards needs allowances alongside the CO2.

cases.question: On a Houston to Rotterdam run our tanker stops at Las Palmas only to take on bunkers. Does that stop count as a port of call and split the voyage for the ETS?
cases.answer: No. Article 3(z) of the ETS Directive defines a port of call as a port where a ship stops to load or unload cargo or to embark or disembark passengers, and excludes stops for the sole purpose of refuelling. Las Palmas therefore does not count, and for the ETS the voyage runs from Houston to Rotterdam: a voyage from a port outside the EU to a Member State port, for which Article 3ga(1) applies surrender requirements to 50 % of the emissions.

cases.question: We already buy voluntary carbon offsets for our fleet. Can we use those credits against our EU ETS obligation instead of buying allowances?
cases.answer: No. Article 12(3)(c) of the ETS Directive requires each shipping company to surrender a number of allowances equal to its total verified emissions for the preceding calendar year, so the obligation can only be met with allowances, and voluntary offset credits do not reduce it.

cases.question: We weren't on the Commission's list of shipping companies and our first ETS voyage was last month. How long do we have to request a maritime operator holding account?
cases.answer: 65 working days from that first voyage. Under Article 15a(1) of the Union Registry Regulation, a shipping company not included in the Commission's list must, within 65 working days of its first voyage falling within the scope of Article 3ga of the ETS Directive, give the relevant national administrator the information set out in Annex VIIa and request it to open a maritime operator holding account.

cases.question: Do we need a special shipping allowance to surrender, or do we use the same EUAs as industry? Could we use the new ETS2 allowances instead?
cases.answer: There is no separate shipping allowance. Article 38(1) of the Union Registry Regulation has the central administrator transfer general allowances for stationary installations and maritime operators to the EU Auction Account, and Article 3(8) defines general allowances as allowances created under Chapter III of Directive 2003/87/EC. ETS2 allowances cannot be used instead: Article 36(5) makes allowances under Chapter IVa of the Directive non-fungible with those under Chapters II and III, and bars them from maritime operator holding accounts.

cases.question: We're a shipowner registered in Singapore. Besides our maritime operator holding account, can we open a trading account in the Union Registry, or can the Member State refuse us for not being based there?
cases.answer: You can request one, but the Member State may impose local conditions. Under Article 16 of the Union Registry Regulation any prospective account holder submits the request to the national administrator with at least the information in Annex IV. The Member State of that national administrator may require, as a condition for opening the account, that the holder has its permanent residence or registration in that Member State, or is registered for VAT there.

cases.question: If we buy more allowances this year than we need, can we keep them for later years, or do they expire?
cases.answer: They do not expire. Article 13 of the ETS Directive makes allowances issued from 1 January 2013 onwards valid indefinitely, so surplus allowances can be kept for later years.

cases.question: Our ISM manager is going to take on ETS compliance for the ships we own. What does the administering authority need to accept that, and who is liable if the paperwork isn't there?
cases.answer: A signed mandate, and without it the shipowner stays liable. Under Article 1 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2599, the ISM company must be duly mandated by the shipowner and give its administering authority a document clearly showing that mandate, signed by both the shipowner and the ISM company. The document gives the name and IMO unique company and registered owner identification number of both parties, the ISM company's country of registration, the shipowner's contact person, the date the mandate applies from, and the IMO number of each ship it covers. If the ISM company cannot provide that document, the shipowner is considered the entity responsible for the ETS obligations.

cases.question: A ship moved from our management to another company on 1 April. Which of us surrenders allowances for its emissions from January to March?
cases.answer: You do, as the previous company. On a change of company, Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 requires the previous company to submit a verified report limited to the period of activities under its responsibility. Under Article 11a(1) each company builds its aggregated emissions data at company level from the emissions reports and these Article 11(2) reports for every ship under its responsibility during the reporting period. Article 12(3)(c) of the ETS Directive then has each shipping company surrender allowances equal to its total verified emissions, so the January to March emissions fall in your total and April to December in the new company's.

cases.question: None of our ships called at an EU port last year, but we still have a maritime operator holding account. What happens to the account for that year?
cases.answer: It is set to excluded. Under Article 9(6b) of the Union Registry Regulation, once the competent authority notifies that a shipping company is no longer included in the EU ETS under Annex I to Directive 2003/87/EC in a given year, the national administrator sets its maritime operator holding account to excluded status, after giving the company prior notice. The account stays excluded until the administering authority notifies that the company is included in the EU ETS again.

cases.question: We moved our company's registration from Cyprus to Greece this year. Does our ETS administering authority change straight away?
cases.answer: No. Under Article 3gf(3), the administering authority responsible for a company on the Commission's list keeps that responsibility regardless of later changes in the company's registration until the change is reflected in an updated list, so Cyprus stays responsible for now. Under Article 3gf(2)(b), the Commission adopts an updated list before 1 February 2026 and every two years after that, reattributing companies that changed their Member State of registration within the Union. Greece then becomes the administering authority, as a company registered in a Member State is administered by that Member State.

cases.question: Our company isn't on the Commission's list of shipping companies and administering authorities. Does that mean the ETS doesn't apply to us?
cases.answer: No. The list under Article 3gf(2) attributes shipping companies to administering authorities, and companies that later perform a maritime transport activity listed in Annex I within the scope of Article 3ga are added in an updated list, adopted before 1 February 2026 and every two years after that. A shipping company not included in the list must, within 65 working days of its first voyage falling within the scope of Article 3ga, give the relevant national administrator the information in Annex VIIa to the Union Registry Regulation and ask it to open a maritime operator holding account (Article 15a(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1122).

cases.question: We're registered in Panama, weren't on the attribution list, and our first ETS voyage was Algeciras to Genoa. Which Member State will administer us?
cases.answer: Spain. Under Article 3gf(1)(c), a shipping company not registered in a Member State that carried out no voyage within the scope of Article 3ga in the preceding four monitoring years is administered by the Member State where one of its ships started or ended its first voyage within that scope. Where that first voyage started at a port of one Member State and ended at a port of another, Article 4 of Regulation (EU) 2023/2599 makes the administering authority the Member State where the voyage started, so the departure from Algeciras decides.

cases.question: What data does the Commission use to decide which Member State a non-EU shipping company is attributed to? Where do the port call counts come from?
cases.answer: Thetis MRV for registration and SafeSeaNet for port calls. Under Article 3 of Regulation (EU) 2023/2599, a shipping company's country of registration is the country recorded in Thetis MRV. Port call data for attributing a company not registered in a Member State are based on data stored in SafeSeaNet, the Union maritime information and exchange system set up by Directive 2002/59/EC. Where the SafeSeaNet data is insufficient, the Commission may use complementary data, such as Automatic Identification System data, stored by other information systems.

cases.question: Does the verifier checking our ETS company-level emissions data need a particular accreditation, and who grants it?
cases.answer: Yes. Under Article 16(1) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757, verifiers that assess the aggregated emissions data at company level, as well as monitoring plans and emissions reports, and that issue verification reports and documents of compliance, must be accredited for activities within the scope of that Regulation. The accreditation is granted by a national accreditation body pursuant to Regulation (EC) No 765/2008.

cases.question: Do Member States have to spend their ETS auction revenue on anything in particular? Does any of it go back into decarbonising shipping or ports?
cases.answer: They must spend it on listed purposes, and maritime decarbonisation is one of them. Under Article 10(3), Member States use auction revenues, other than those used to compensate indirect carbon costs or entered in the Union budget as own resources, or the equivalent in financial value, for one or more listed purposes. Point (f) covers measures to decarbonise the maritime sector, including the energy efficiency of ships, ports, innovative technologies and infrastructure, sustainable alternative fuels such as hydrogen and ammonia produced from renewables, and zero-emission propulsion technologies. Article 10(3) does not reserve any revenue for shipping, but under Article 3ga(3) the revenue from the extra share of allowances attributed until 31 December 2030 to Member States with more than 15 shipping companies per million inhabitants should be used for point (g) with regard to the maritime sector and for points (f) and (i).

cases.question: Our ro-ro runs between Las Palmas and Cádiz. Do we have to surrender ETS allowances for those voyages?
cases.answer: Not for emissions released until 31 December 2030. Las Palmas is in the Canary Islands, an outermost region under Article 349 TFEU. Under Article 12(3-b), no obligation to surrender allowances arises for emissions released until 31 December 2030 from voyages between a port in an outermost region of a Member State and a port in the same Member State, or from those ships' activities within a port in relation to such voyages. Las Palmas to Cádiz is such a voyage, as both ports are in Spain.

cases.question: We operate the Piraeus to Limassol passenger ferry under the Greece-Cyprus public service contract. Do we have to surrender allowances for those voyages?
cases.answer: Not for emissions released until 31 December 2030. Article 12(3-c) lets the Commission, at the joint request of two Member States, provide that Member States treat the surrender obligation and the penalties in Article 16 as satisfied and take no action for voyages by passenger or ro-pax ships under a transnational public service contract or obligation connecting them, and for those ships' activities in port in relation to such voyages. Article 1(b) of Implementing Decision (EU) 2023/2895 does this for the contracts listed in its Annex II, which lists the public service contract for the passenger maritime link between Cyprus and Greece connecting Piraeus, Larnaca and Limassol.

cases.question: All our ships are island ferries covered by the ETS surrender derogation. Do we still have to monitor and report their emissions?
cases.answer: Yes. The island derogation in Article 12(3-d) only has Member States treat the surrender obligation in Article 12(3), point (c), and the penalties in Article 16 as satisfied and take no action against the company. Under Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2015/757, emissions under the derogation are multiplied by zero in the total to be reported under the ETS, but the company must still monitor, per voyage, the ports and times of departure and arrival, the amount and emission factor of each fuel, the greenhouse gas emissions, the distance travelled and the time spent at sea. Where all of a ship's emissions in a reporting period fall under the derogations and the ship performs more than 300 voyages in that period according to its schedule, that information need not be monitored per voyage.

cases.question: If we switch our container ships to a certified sustainable biofuel blend, do we still need allowances for the emissions from the bio share?
cases.answer: Not for its CO2. Under Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2015/757, where a company uses a fuel complying with the sustainability and greenhouse gas emission saving criteria for biomass in Directive (EU) 2018/2001, the CO2 emission factor of the biomass fraction of the fuel is zero in the emissions reported under the ETS. Only the CO2 emission factor is zeroed, so methane and nitrous oxide from the fuel still count, and the ETS covers those gases for maritime transport from 1 January 2026 under Annex I to Directive 2003/87/EC.

cases.question: If we fit onboard carbon capture and deliver the CO2 to a storage site, do we still have to surrender allowances for it?
cases.answer: No, provided the storage site is permitted. Under Article 12(3a), no obligation to surrender allowances arises for emissions verified as captured and transported for permanent storage to a facility with a permit in force under Directive 2009/31/EC on the geological storage of carbon dioxide. For ships, Annex II to Regulation (EU) 2015/757 multiplies CO2 emissions within the scope of Article 12(3a) by zero when calculating the emissions to be reported under the ETS.

cases.question: We run a 6,000 GT fish-processing vessel and a government survey ship that both call at EU ports. Is either of them caught by EU MRV?
cases.answer: No, neither, provided the survey ship is not used commercially. Article 2(2) of the MRV Regulation says it does not apply to fish-catching or fish-processing ships, so the fish-processing vessel is out even though it is above 5,000 GT. The same paragraph excludes government ships used for non-commercial purposes, which takes out the survey ship as long as it is used for non-commercial purposes.

cases.question: Our 2,500 GT crew/supply vessel works North Sea projects out of Esbjerg. Does EU MRV apply to it, and from when?
cases.answer: Yes, from 1 January 2025. Annex I lists crew/supply vessels among the ships, other than icebreakers, designed or certified to perform service activities offshore or at offshore installations. Article 2(1a) extends the Regulation from 1 January 2025 to offshore ships below 5 000 but not below 400 gross tonnage, for emissions on voyages from their last port of call to a port of call under a Member State's jurisdiction, from such a port to their next port of call, and within those ports.

cases.question: Our general cargo ship discharges in Rotterdam, then sails empty to Brazil to load grain. Do we have to monitor and report that ballast leg under MRV?
cases.answer: Yes. Rotterdam is a port of call because the ship stops there to unload cargo (Article 3, point (z) of Directive 2003/87/EC, which the MRV Regulation adopts in its Article 3(b)), and under Article 3(c) a voyage is any movement of a ship that originates from or terminates in a port of call. Article 4(1) requires companies to monitor and report for any voyages to or from a port under a Member State's jurisdiction, so the ballast leg counts like any other. For a general cargo ship, Article 3(f) of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/1928 sets cargo carried at zero for ballast voyages.

cases.question: We leave Antwerp, do a ship-to-ship transfer outside Houston port limits, then discharge in South Korea. Where does our MRV voyage end?
cases.answer: In South Korea. Article 3(b) of the MRV Regulation takes its definition of port of call from Article 3, point (z) of Directive 2003/87/EC, and that definition excludes ship-to-ship transfers carried out outside ports. The transfer off Houston is therefore not a port of call and does not end the voyage. The voyage covered under Article 2(1) runs from Antwerp to the next port of call, the discharge port in South Korea.

cases.question: Do the emissions from our ship while alongside in Hamburg count under MRV, and do they have to be reported separately from the voyage?
cases.answer: Yes, and yes. Article 2(1) covers emissions released within ports of call under a Member State's jurisdiction as well as on voyages. Article 10(f) makes greenhouse gas emissions within ports under a Member State's jurisdiction at berth a parameter of their own in annual monitoring, and Part A of Annex I requires fuel consumption at berth in those ports to be calculated separately. Under Article 11(3)(d) the emissions report includes the results of the annual monitoring of the Article 10 parameters.

cases.question: Our tanker loads in Houston and sails to Rotterdam. For MRV, do emissions start counting while we're loading in Houston or only once we leave the berth?
cases.answer: Only once you leave the berth. Article 2(1) covers emissions on the voyage from the last port of call to a port of call under a Member State's jurisdiction, and emissions within ports only for ports of call under a Member State's jurisdiction, so time loading alongside in Houston is outside it. Part A of Annex II records each voyage from the date and hour of departure from berth to arrival at berth.

cases.question: By what date each year do we have to submit the verified MRV emissions report for each ship, and who do we send it to?
cases.answer: By 31 March. From 2025, Article 11(1) requires companies to submit, for each ship under their responsibility, an emissions report for the entire reporting period of the previous year, verified as satisfactory by a verifier, to the administering authority responsible, to the authorities of the flag State for ships flying the flag of a Member State, and to the Commission. The administering authority responsible may require the report earlier than 31 March, but not earlier than 28 February.

cases.question: One of our ships didn't call at any EU port all last year. Does it still need an MRV document of compliance for that year?
cases.answer: No. Article 18 requires a valid document of compliance on board only for ships that carried out voyages during the reporting period, and the Regulation covers only voyages to or from, and time within, ports of call under a Member State's jurisdiction (Article 2(1)). A ship with no such voyages in the year needs no document of compliance for it.

cases.question: We sold a ship to another company halfway through the year. What MRV report do we owe for our part of the year, who gets it, and by when?
cases.answer: A verified partial report. Under Article 11(2), where there is a change of company the previous company must submit a verified report covering the same elements as the annual emissions report, limited to the period of the activities carried out under its responsibility. It goes to the administering authority responsible, to the flag State authorities for ships flying the flag of a Member State, to the new company and to the Commission. It is due as close as practicable to the day the change is completed and no later than three months after it.

cases.question: The registered owner is taking over as the responsible company for one of our ships mid-year. Does the monitoring plan need changing, and does the verifier have to reassess it?
cases.answer: The plan must be modified, but the verifier does not assess that change. Article 7(2)(a) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 requires the monitoring plan to be modified where a change of company occurs, and Article 7(3) requires the proposed modification to be notified to the verifier without undue delay. Article 7(4) subjects only modifications under points (b) to (d) to the verifier's assessment, so under Article 75(1) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 the modified plan goes to the administering authority responsible once the verifier has been notified. That authority approves it under Article 7(5), and under Article 76(2) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 the company must give it evidence of the change of company and, where the administering authority is not the same, an indication with supporting evidence of whether the plan had been approved before the change.

cases.question: Our ship left Singapore on 20 December and arrived in Rotterdam on 15 January. Which year's MRV report do the voyage emissions go in?
cases.answer: Both years. Article 3(m) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 defines the reporting period as 1 January to 31 December of a given year, and for voyages starting and ending in two different years the respective data are accounted under the year concerned. So the data for the December part of the voyage go in that year's report and the data for the January part go in the next year's.

cases.question: Can our MRV verifier do the site visit virtually instead of coming in person, and is there a limit on that?
cases.answer: Yes, within limits. Under Article 18(6) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 the verifier may carry out a virtual site visit where its risk analysis shows that it already has sufficient understanding of the ship's monitoring and reporting systems, that the system is simple enough not to need a physical visit, or that it can obtain and assess all requisite information remotely, or where serious, extraordinary and unforeseeable circumstances outside the company's control prevent a physical visit. Except in those circumstances, it may not carry out a virtual site visit if no physical site visit took place in the three reporting periods immediately preceding the current one.

cases.question: We have twelve sister ships. Can we submit one MRV monitoring plan for the whole fleet, or does each ship need its own?
cases.answer: Each ship needs its own. Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 requires companies to submit a monitoring plan for each of their ships, and Article 6(3) makes each plan a complete and transparent documentation of the monitoring method for the ship concerned, starting with that ship's name, IMO identification number, port of registry or home port and shipowner.

cases.question: Our monitoring plan is written in Greek. Is that acceptable to the verifier, or does it have to be in English?
cases.answer: The plan can be in Greek, but you must also give the verifier an English translation. Article 4(1) of Regulation (EU) 2023/2917 requires companies to provide the verifier with their ship's monitoring plan and, where the plan is in a language other than English, an English translation of it.

cases.question: What does an MRV monitoring plan actually have to contain, and do we have to include procedures for navigating through ice?
cases.answer: At least ten elements, and the ice information is optional. Article 6(3) of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 requires the plan to be complete and transparent documentation of the ship's monitoring method containing at least: the ship's identification and type (name, IMO number, port of registry or home port, shipowner), the company's name, contact person and IMO unique company and registered owner identification number, a description of the emission sources on board (main and auxiliary engines, gas turbines, boilers and inert gas generators) and the fuel types used, the procedures for updating the list of emission sources and for monitoring the completeness of the list of voyages, the procedures for monitoring fuel consumption (the Annex I method for each emission source, measurement of fuel uplifts and fuel in tanks, density and fuel measurement uncertainty), the emission factors for each fuel type or the methodology for alternative fuels, the procedures for determining distance, cargo carried and passengers, and time at sea per voyage, the method for surrogate data to close data gaps, and a revision record sheet. Under Article 6(4) the plan may also contain the ship's ice class and the procedures for determining and recording the distance travelled and time spent at sea when navigating through ice.

cases.question: Do we submit our MRV monitoring plan through THETIS-MRV, and is there a set template we have to use?
cases.answer: Yes to both. Article 1 of Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2449 requires companies submitting the monitoring plan under Article 6 of Regulation (EU) 2015/757 to use the electronic version of the template available in THETIS-MRV, the system operated by the European Maritime Safety Agency, and that template contains the information set out in Annex I to the Implementing Regulation.

cases.question: We're a verification company based in the Netherlands. Which accreditation body do we apply to for MRV verifier accreditation, and can we go to another country's body instead?
cases.answer: The Dutch national accreditation body, as a rule.
